read.when: Always: every solution is loops and conditions, and complexity tells you whether it's fast enough before you submit.
idea: Count how many times the innermost line runs as the input grows: one loop over n is O(n), a loop inside a loop is O(n²).
About 10⁸ simple operations run in a second, so with n = 10⁵ an O(n²) idea is too slow and you need O(n) or O(n log n).
mistakes: Off-by-one loop bounds (< vs <=) and forgetting the empty or single-element input.
Integer overflow when sums or products pass about 2·10⁹: use long long (C++) or long (Java).

read.when: The input is a list of numbers and you need to scan, count, rearrange or update it.
idea: One pass with a few variables (a running count, the best so far) solves most easy array problems in O(n).
To change an array in place, keep a write index that only moves when you keep an element.
mistakes: Reading a[i + 1] or a[i - 1] past the ends of the array.
Changing the array while you still need its old values: copy them first or write behind the read index.

read.when: The input is text: words, characters, palindromes, prefixes.
idea: A string is an array of characters, so the array patterns (one pass, indexes from both ends) carry over.
Build new strings with a list or StringBuilder, then join once, instead of adding to a string in a loop.
mistakes: Mixing up characters and their codes: 'a' - 'a' is 0, and upper and lower case differ.
Repeated string concatenation in a loop, which can quietly turn O(n) into O(n²).

steps.title: Hashing
steps.subtitle: Sets and maps for instant lookups

read.when: You keep asking "have I seen this before?" or "how many times does this appear?"
idea: A hash set answers "seen it?" and a hash map stores a count or an index, both in O(1) on average.
Two Sum's trick: for each number, look up the partner you need before you store the number itself.
mistakes: Reading a missing key: in C++ map[k] silently creates it, so use count or find first.
Using a hash map where a 26-slot array would do for lowercase letters.

steps.title: Two Pointers
steps.subtitle: Two indexes moving through the input

read.when: The array is sorted, or you compare things from both ends (palindromes, pairs that add up to a target).
idea: Start one index at each end and move the one that can only make the answer better, so each step drops a candidate.
That turns the O(n²) check of every pair into one O(n) pass.
mistakes: Stopping at left < right versus left <= right: decide whether both may point at the same element.
Using it on unsorted input where moving a pointer doesn't tell you anything.

read.when: The question asks about a contiguous subarray or substring: longest, shortest, or the best sum of size k.
idea: Keep a window [left, right]: grow it by moving right, and shrink it from the left only when it breaks the rule.
Update the window's sum or counts as elements enter and leave, instead of recomputing them each time.
mistakes: Recomputing the whole window on every step, which is O(n·k) again.
Forgetting to undo the leaving element's effect (its count or its share of the sum) when left moves.

steps.title: Stack and Queue
steps.subtitle: Last in first out, first in first out

read.when: Things open and close in matching pairs (brackets, undo), or each element needs the next greater one.
idea: A stack holds what's still open: push when something starts, pop when it ends, and the top is always the most recent.
A queue serves in arrival order, which is what BFS needs later.
mistakes: Popping or reading the top of an empty stack.
Not checking that the stack is empty at the end (an unclosed bracket is still invalid).

read.when: The data is sorted, or the answer has a yes/no test that flips once (too small … big enough).
idea: Look at the middle, decide which half can still hold the answer, and throw the other half away: O(log n).
Write the loop around one invariant, like "the answer is always inside [lo, hi]".
mistakes: Endless loops from mixing up lo = mid with lo = mid + 1.
Overflow in (lo + hi) / 2 on big values: use lo + (hi - lo) / 2.

read.when: A problem is made of smaller copies of itself: a tree, a sequence like Fibonacci, all choices of something.
idea: Trust the function: assume it already works for smaller inputs, and write only how to combine those answers.
Every recursive function needs a base case that stops it, checked before the recursive calls.
mistakes: A missing or wrong base case, which recurses forever (stack overflow).
Recomputing the same calls again and again (plain Fibonacci is exponential); that's what DP fixes later.

read.when: The input is a linked list, or you need cheap inserts and removes in the middle of a sequence.
idea: Walk with a pointer, and keep a prev pointer whenever you need to relink (reversing a list is just that).
A dummy head node removes the special case of changing the first node.
mistakes: Losing the rest of the list by overwriting next before saving it.
Not handling an empty list or a single node.

read.when: The input is a tree, or data has a parent and child shape (folders, expressions).
idea: Most tree answers are recursion: solve the left subtree, solve the right one, combine at the node.
Preorder, inorder and postorder only differ in when you look at the node: before, between or after its children.
mistakes: Forgetting the null child, which is the base case of almost every tree function.
Mixing up depth (from the root down) and height (from the node down to a leaf).

read.when: Things are connected: cities and roads, cells of a grid, people and friendships.
idea: DFS goes as deep as it can before backing up (recursion or a stack); BFS goes level by level with a queue.
Mark a node visited the moment you add it, so it's processed once: O(nodes + edges).
mistakes: Not marking visited, or marking it too late, so nodes get queued twice or the search loops forever.
Running off the grid: check row and column bounds before reading a neighbouring cell.

read.when: A locally best choice never needs to be undone: biggest coin first, earliest-ending meeting first.
idea: Sort by the right key, then make the obvious choice at each step and never look back.
Before coding, try to break it with a small counterexample; if you can, it needs DP instead.
mistakes: Sorting by the wrong key (start time instead of end time is the classic one).
Trusting a greedy idea that only works on the sample tests.

read.when: Recursion would solve the same subproblem many times, and you want a count, a minimum or a maximum.
idea: Define dp[i] in one sentence ("the number of ways to reach step i"), then write how it's built from smaller i.
Fill the table from the base cases up, or keep the recursion and cache each answer (memoization).
mistakes: A fuzzy definition of dp[i]: if you can't say it in one sentence, the transition will be wrong.
Wrong base cases or table size (n versus n + 1).
